claim: Mice learned a visual change detection task with a set of eight natural scene images.
source: Mice learned a visual change detection task with a set of eight natural scene images.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and describes the experimental design.

claim: During 2-photon imaging experiments, mice performed the task with familiar images and three sets of novel images.
source: Subsequently, during 2-photon imaging experiments, mice performed the task with these familiar images and three sets of novel images.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: VIP cells were stimulus-driven by novel images.
source: VIP cells were stimulus-driven by novel images but were suppressed by familiar stimuli and showed ramping activity when expected stimuli were omitted from a temporally predictable sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: VIP cells were suppressed by familiar stimuli.
source: VIP cells were stimulus-driven by novel images but were suppressed by familiar stimuli and showed ramping activity when expected stimuli were omitted from a temporally predictable sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: VIP cells showed ramping activity when expected stimuli were omitted from a temporally predictable sequence.
source: VIP cells were stimulus-driven by novel images but were suppressed by familiar stimuli and showed ramping activity when expected stimuli were omitted from a temporally predictable sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The temporal dynamics of VIP activity differed markedly between novel and familiar images.
source: Strikingly, the temporal dynamics of VIP activity differed markedly between novel and familiar images
evidence: This is a key finding emphasized in the abstract.

claim: Visual experience can modify cortical representations, including changes in gain, selectivity, correlations, and population dynamics.
source: Visual experience can modify cortical representations, including changes in gain, selectivity, correlations, and population dynamics (Jurjut et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2018; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Poort et al., 2015; Weskelblatt and Niell, 2019; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Sensory and behavioral experience can lead to the emergence of predictive activity in the visual cortex including reward anticipation.
source: Moreover, sensory and behavioral experience can lead to the emergence of predictive activity in the visual cortex including reward anticipation (Poort et al., 2015; Shuler and Bear, 2006), spatial expectation (Fiser et al., 2016; Saleem et al., 2018), anticipatory recall (Gavornik and Bear, 2014; Xu et al., 2012) and prediction error signals (Fiser et al., 2016; Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VIP cells receive long-range projections from frontal areas.
source: VIP cells receive long-range projections from frontal areas (Lee et al., 2013; Wall et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014) as well as cholinergic and noradrenergic inputs (Alitto and Dan, 2013; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: VIP cells are highly active during states of arousal.
source: VIP cells are highly active during states of arousal (Fu et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2014), are modulated by task engagement (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017), and are responsive to behavioral reinforcement (Krabbe et al., 2019; Letzkus et al., 2011; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: VIP cells primarily inhibit somatostatin (SST) cells in the local cortical circuitry.
source: In the local cortical circuitry, VIP cells primarily inhibit another major class of inhibitory interneuron, somatostatin (SST) cells (Lee et al., 2013; Munoz et al., 2017; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013), which can result in disinhibition of excitatory neurons (Fu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Letzkus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mice were trained on a go/no-go visual change detection task with natural scene stimuli.
source: We trained mice on a go/no-go visual change detection task with natural scene stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Images were presented for 250 ms followed by 500 ms gray screen.
source: In this task, mice see a continuous stream of repeatedly presented images (250 ms stimulus presentation followed by 500 ms gray screen; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation parameters used in the task.

claim: On 'go' trials, the image identity changes and mice report the change by licking a reward spout within 750 ms.
source: On 'go' trials, the image identity changes and mice report the change by licking a reward spout within 750 ms (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task structure.

claim: Approximately 5% of all image presentations were randomly omitted.
source: To test whether expectation signals exist in the visual cortex due to the temporal regularity of this task, we randomly omitted ~5% of all image presentations (not including image changes to avoid interfering with behavior performance).
evidence: This describes an experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: Mice viewed each of the eight images from the familiar set 10,350 times on average prior to the 2-photon imaging stage.
source: On average, mice viewed each of the eight images from the familiar set 10,350 times prior to the 2-photon imaging stage (range: 944–26,784 individual stimulus presentations per image).
evidence: This quantifies the extent of familiarity with the training images.

claim: Hit rates, false alarm rates, and reaction times were similar across image sets.
source: Hit rates, false alarm rates, and reaction times (lick latency) were similar across image sets (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study.

claim: There was no difference in running behavior between novel and familiar image sessions.
source: There was no difference in running behavior between novel and familiar image sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that behavioral differences do not explain neural differences.

claim: Licking behavior around the time of omission was similar across image sets.
source: Licking behavior around the time of omission was also similar across image sets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing behavioral consistency across conditions.

claim: On average 181 ± 77 (mean ± SD) Slc17a7+ cells were imaged per session.
source: On average we imaged 181 ± 77 (mean ± SD) Slc17a7+ cells or 15 ± 10 VIP+ cells per session.
evidence: This describes the sample size of recorded neurons.

claim: On average 15 ± 10 VIP+ cells were imaged per session.
source: On average we imaged 181 ± 77 (mean ± SD) Slc17a7+ cells or 15 ± 10 VIP+ cells per session.
evidence: This describes the sample size of recorded neurons.

claim: Measurements were made in primary visual cortex (VISp) and one higher visual area (VISal).
source: Measurements were made in primary visual cortex (VISp) and one higher visual area (VISal) but we did not observe major differences between these two areas, so the datasets were combined for the analyses reported here.
evidence: This describes the brain regions recorded from in the study.

claim: No major differences were observed between VISp and VISal, so the datasets were combined.
source: Measurements were made in primary visual cortex (VISp) and one higher visual area (VISal) but we did not observe major differences between these two areas, so the datasets were combined for the analyses reported here.
evidence: This justifies combining data from two brain regions.

claim: Excitatory cells typically responded to only one or a few images in each set.
source: Excitatory cells typically responded to only one or a few images in each set, showing fluorescence increases after stimulus onset or sometimes after stimulus offset (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the response properties of excitatory neurons.

claim: VIP cells were less image selective than excitatory cells.
source: VIP cells were less image selective and showed correlated fluctuations in activity (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This describes the response properties of VIP neurons.

claim: VIP cells showed correlated fluctuations in activity.
source: VIP cells were less image selective and showed correlated fluctuations in activity (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This describes the response properties of VIP neurons.

claim: Novel images generated stimulus-locked activity in VIP cells.
source: Novel images generated stimulus-locked activity in VIP cells (Figure 2D), but this was reduced or absent with familiar images.
evidence: This is a key finding comparing VIP responses to novel vs familiar stimuli.

claim: During familiar image sessions many VIP neurons had ramping activity that preceded stimulus presentation and decayed after stimulus onset.
source: Instead, during familiar image sessions many VIP neurons had ramping activity that preceded stimulus presentation and decayed after stimulus onset (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a key finding about VIP dynamics with familiar stimuli.

claim: VIP ramping responses were more pronounced when an image presentation was omitted.
source: These ramping responses were even more pronounced when an image presentation was omitted (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This describes VIP responses to stimulus omissions.

claim: VIP cells showed little activity during the omission of novel image presentations.
source: In contrast, VIP cells showed little activity during the omission of novel image presentations (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This describes VIP responses to omissions of novel stimuli.

claim: Both excitatory and VIP inhibitory populations had reduced activity levels with familiar images.
source: Quantifying each cell's mean response to its preferred image in each set revealed that both excitatory and VIP inhibitory populations had reduced activity levels with familiar images (Figure 3B, p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A for both excitatory and VIP inhibitory populations, except comparison between A-C for excitatory neurons where p=0.05, Welch's t-test with Bonferroni correction, see Materials and methods for detailed description of statistics used throughout).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: Both VIP and excitatory cells showed increased stimulus omission activity in familiar image sessions.
source: Both VIP and excitatory cells showed increased stimulus omission activity in familiar image sessions (Figure 3C, p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: The fraction of cells that were significantly more responsive during image presentations compared to stimulus omission was higher for novel image sets for both cell classes.
source: The fraction of cells that were significantly more responsive during image presentations compared to stimulus omission was higher for novel image sets for both cell classes (Figure 3D, p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: 55% of VIP cells were omission responsive with the familiar image set compared to 6–20% for novel image sets.
source: While excitatory cells had a small but significant increase in the fraction of omission responsive cells (2.3% for image set A versus <1% for image sets B-D), a large fraction of VIP cells were omission responsive with the familiar image set compared to novel image sets (55% for image set A, 6–20% for image sets B-D) (Figure 3E, for VIP: p<0.008 for A-B and A-C, p=0.03 for A-D; for excitatory: p=0.01 for A-B and A-C, p=0.05 for A-D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: There is a trade-off between image responsiveness and omission activity in VIP cells.
source: This indicates a trade-off between image responsiveness and omission activity in VIP cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing inverse relationship between image and omission responses.

claim: The responses of individual excitatory neurons to natural images were more selective for familiar compared to novel stimuli.
source: We also observed that the responses of individual excitatory neurons to natural images were more selective for familiar compared to novel stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding about single cell selectivity.

claim: Excitatory populations had higher lifetime sparseness values for the familiar image set compared to the novel image sets.
source: Excitatory populations had higher lifetime sparseness values for the familiar image set compared to the novel image sets (p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A and for B-C for excitatory cells), and excitatory cells were typically sparser than VIP cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: Excitatory cells were typically sparser than VIP cells.
source: Excitatory populations had higher lifetime sparseness values for the familiar image set compared to the novel image sets (p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A and for B-C for excitatory cells), and excitatory cells were typically sparser than VIP cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a comparison between cell types.

claim: While overall population activity levels were reduced for familiar images, single cell selectivity was sharpened.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that while overall population activity levels were reduced for familiar images, single cell selectivity was sharpened.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about population vs single cell responses.

claim: The excitatory population showed a sharp increase in activity following stimulus onset.
source: The excitatory population showed a sharp increase in activity following stimulus onset, and while familiar images evoked a smaller population response magnitude, the timing of activity was similar across novel and familiar image sets (Figure 4A, left panel).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of excitatory responses.

claim: The timing of excitatory activity was similar across novel and familiar image sets.
source: The excitatory population showed a sharp increase in activity following stimulus onset, and while familiar images evoked a smaller population response magnitude, the timing of activity was similar across novel and familiar image sets (Figure 4A, left panel).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of excitatory responses.

claim: With novel images, the VIP population response increased following stimulus onset.
source: In contrast, VIP population dynamics were very different between familiar and novel images sets. With novel images, the VIP population response increased following stimulus onset, but with familiar images, VIP activity ramped up during the inter-stimulus interval and peaked at the time of stimulus onset (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes VIP temporal dynamics with novel stimuli.

claim: With familiar images, VIP activity ramped up during the inter-stimulus interval and peaked at the time of stimulus onset.
source: In contrast, VIP population dynamics were very different between familiar and novel images sets. With novel images, the VIP population response increased following stimulus onset, but with familiar images, VIP activity ramped up during the inter-stimulus interval and peaked at the time of stimulus onset (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes VIP temporal dynamics with familiar stimuli.

claim: Pre-stimulus ramping activity was readily apparent in individual VIP cells but was rare in excitatory cells.
source: This pre-stimulus ramping activity was readily apparent in individual VIP cells but was rare in excitatory cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This compares the prevalence of ramping between cell types.

claim: The distribution of peak response times across VIP cells was shifted earlier in time for familiar versus novel images sets.
source: Consistent with this effect, the distribution of peak response times across VIP cells was shifted earlier in time for familiar versus novel images sets (Figure 4C, p<0.008 for all image set comparisons except B-C for VIP cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: The distribution of the stimulus ramp index was shifted towards positive values for novel images.
source: The distribution of the stimulus ramp index was shifted towards positive values for novel images, consistent with increased image responsiveness (see marginal distributions in Figure 4D, p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A, as well as for B-D and C-D for excitatory cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: The distribution of the pre-stimulus ramp index values was shifted towards positive values for VIP cells with the familiar image set.
source: The distribution of the pre-stimulus ramp index values was also shifted towards positive values for VIP cells with the familiar image set, indicating an increase in pre-stimulus ramping (see marginals distributions in Figure 4D, p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A, as well as for B-C and C-D for excitatory cells and B-D for VIP cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: The values of the ramp index for the pre-stimulus and stimulus periods were inversely correlated.
source: The values of the ramp index for the pre-stimulus and stimulus periods were inversely correlated (Figure 4D; VIP: r = −0.69, p<0.005; excitatory: r = −0.36, p<0.005; linear least-squares regression fit across all cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: There is a tradeoff between stimulus-driven activity and inter-stimulus ramping, particularly in VIP cells.
source: This indicates a tradeoff between stimulus-driven activity and inter-stimulus ramping, particularly in VIP cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inverse correlation between stimulus and pre-stimulus ramp indices.

claim: During novel image sessions, most VIP cells were stimulus-driven (~80%).
source: VIP inhibitory cells showed a larger difference across image sets: during novel image sessions, most cells were stimulus-driven (<80%), whereas during familiar image sessions, the majority of VIP cells (60%) were stimulus-suppressed and showed pre-stimulus ramping (Figure 4E,F right panels; p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: During familiar image sessions, the majority of VIP cells (60%) were stimulus-suppressed and showed pre-stimulus ramping.
source: VIP inhibitory cells showed a larger difference across image sets: during novel image sessions, most cells were stimulus-driven (<80%), whereas during familiar image sessions, the majority of VIP cells (60%) were stimulus-suppressed and showed pre-stimulus ramping (Figure 4E,F right panels; p<0.008 for all comparisons with image set A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: VIP cells exhibited clear pre-stimulus ramping even when the mouse was stationary.
source: We found that VIP cells exhibited clear pre-stimulus ramping even when the mouse stationary (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that locomotion does not explain VIP ramping.

claim: The pattern of running behavior was similar for novel and familiar sessions, despite a clear difference in VIP cell dynamics.
source: Moreover, we examined stimulus-triggered changes in running speed and found that the pattern of running behavior was similar for novel and familiar sessions, despite a clear difference in VIP cell dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that locomotion does not explain VIP dynamics.

claim: The stimulus-triggered dynamics of pupil area changes were relatively flat and did not match the VIP cell dynamics.
source: We found that in novel sessions pupil area was slightly larger on average, but the stimulus-triggered dynamics of pupil area changes were relatively flat and did not match the VIP cell dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that arousal does not explain VIP dynamics.

claim: VIP ramping activity does not trivially reflect locomotor or pupil dynamics.
source: Together these analyses demonstrate that VIP ramping activity does not trivially reflect locomotor or pupil dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses.

claim: VIP population activity continued to ramp up during stimulus omission, until the subsequent stimulus presentation.
source: Strikingly, VIP population activity continued to ramp up during stimulus omission, until the subsequent stimulus presentation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes VIP responses to stimulus omissions.

claim: Activity following stimulus omission was much stronger during familiar compared to novel image sessions.
source: Activity following stimulus omission was much stronger during familiar compared to novel image sessions (Figure 5B; p<0.008 for all comparisons except A-C for VIP).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: Very few excitatory cells showed increases in activity following stimulus omission.
source: Visualizing mean omission related activity for all cells as a heatmap for each image set confirmed that very few excitatory cells showed increases in activity following stimulus omission and were primarily active during the stimulus presentations before and after omission (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes excitatory responses to omissions.

claim: Most VIP cells showed a dramatic increase in activity following stimulus omission for familiar stimuli.
source: In contrast, most VIP cells showed a dramatic increase in activity following stimulus omission for familiar stimuli (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes VIP responses to omissions of familiar stimuli.

claim: Omission ramping activity was present even when the mice were not running.
source: We found that omission ramping activity was present even when the mice were not running (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that locomotion does not explain omission responses.

claim: Omission-triggered pupil dynamics were similar during novel and familiar sessions.
source: Moreover, omission-triggered pupil dynamics were similar during novel and familiar sessions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that arousal does not explain omission responses.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the strength of pre-stimulus and omission ramping for VIP cells.
source: We found a positive correlation between the strength of pre-stimulus and omission ramping for VIP cells (Figure 5D; r = 0.49, p<0.005, linear least-squares regression across all VIP cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: Pre-stimulus and omission dynamics were not correlated in excitatory cells.
source: In contrast, pre-stimulus and omission dynamics were not correlated in excitatory cells.
evidence: This is a comparison between cell types.

claim: Extended experience with a set of images resulted in reduced overall activity levels in both excitatory and VIP cells.
source: Extended experience with a set of images resulted in reduced overall activity levels in both excitatory and VIP cells.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: VIP cells exhibited distinct activity dynamics when tested with familiar versus novel images.
source: Strikingly, VIP cells exhibited distinct activity dynamics when tested with familiar versus novel images.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: Novel images drove stimulus-locked activity in VIP cells.
source: Novel images drove stimulus-locked activity in VIP cells, whereas with familiar images VIP cells had ramping activity during the inter-stimulus interval and were suppressed by stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: With familiar images VIP cells had ramping activity during the inter-stimulus interval and were suppressed by stimulus onset.
source: Novel images drove stimulus-locked activity in VIP cells, whereas with familiar images VIP cells had ramping activity during the inter-stimulus interval and were suppressed by stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: VIP ramping responses continued increasing when stimuli were omitted from the expected stimulus sequence.
source: Moreover, these ramping responses continued increasing when stimuli were omitted from the expected stimulus sequence.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: The magnitude of VIP omission-related activity was several times larger than stimulus-driven activity.
source: The magnitude of VIP omission-related activity was several times larger than stimulus-driven activity, indicating these are meaningful signals that could strongly influence network activity.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: VIP omission-related activity represents meaningful signals that could strongly influence network activity.
source: The magnitude of VIP omission-related activity was several times larger than stimulus-driven activity, indicating these are meaningful signals that could strongly influence network activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the magnitude of omission responses.

claim: This represents a major experience-dependent cell type-specific change in response dynamics in sensory cortex.
source: This represents a major experience-dependent cell type-specific change in response dynamics in sensory cortex.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Predictive processing theories posit that the brain constructs an internal model of the environment based on experience.
source: This family of theories posits that the brain constructs an internal model of the environment based on experience, and that incoming sensory information is compared with learned expectations to continually update the model (de Lange et al., 2018; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Lochmann and Deneve, 2011; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: This is a description of theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: As stimuli become familiar with learning, predictive signals may suppress bottom-up input, resulting in a sparser code.
source: As stimuli become familiar with learning, predictive signals may suppress bottom-up input, resulting in a sparser code.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from predictive coding framework.

claim: Novel or surprising stimuli are expected to robustly drive neural activity, signaling deviations from learned predictions.
source: On the other hand, novel or surprising stimuli are expected to robustly drive neural activity, signaling deviations from learned predictions.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from predictive coding framework.

claim: Previous studies have shown reductions in activity with experience.
source: Previous studies have shown reductions in activity with experience (Anderson et al., 2008; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Mruczek and Sheinberg, 2007; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012), and also novelty enhancement (Hamm and Yuste, 2016; Homann et al., 2017; Ranganath and Rainer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reduced activity for highly familiar stimuli can efficiently code predictable stimuli, utilizing a smaller population of cells to represent learned information.
source: Reduced activity for highly familiar stimuli can efficiently code predictable stimuli, utilizing a smaller population of cells to represent learned information (LeMessurier and Feldman, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Enhanced activity for novel stimuli could aid detection of salient and behaviorally meaningful events by augmenting output to downstream targets and facilitating associative plasticity.
source: On the other hand, enhanced activity for novel stimuli could aid detection of salient and behaviorally meaningful events by augmenting output to downstream targets and facilitating associative plasticity (Ranganath and Rainer, 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The results demonstrating reduced activity with long-term experience and enhancement with novelty are consistent with the predictive coding framework.
source: Our results demonstrating reduced activity with long-term experience and enhancement with novelty are consistent with the predictive coding framework.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theory.

claim: Increased VIP activity in response to novel images may serve to disinhibit excitatory cell responses to novel stimuli via the VIP-SST disinhibitory circuit.
source: Increased VIP activity in response to novel images may serve to disinhibit excitatory cell responses to novel stimuli (via the VIP-SST disinhibitory circuit).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: When stimuli are familiar, VIP cells are suppressed by image presentation, which may permit increased inhibition of excitatory neurons by SST or PV cells, thus increasing the sparseness of stimulus representations.
source: When stimuli are familiar, VIP cells are suppressed by image presentation, which may permit increased inhibition of excitatory neurons by SST or PV cells, thus increasing the sparseness of stimulus representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: VIP ramping activity may reflect the temporal structure of the behavioral task such that these signals encode predictions about stimulus timing or reward expectation, or serve as a temporal attention signal.
source: One possibility is that this activity reflects the temporal structure of the behavioral task such that these signals encode predictions about stimulus timing or reward expectation, or serve as a temporal attention signal (Nobre and van Ede, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: An early study showed that pairing visual stimulation with a temporally predictable reward produces reward timing signals in visual cortex.
source: An early example showed that pairing visual stimulation with a temporally predictable reward produces reward timing signals in visual cortex (Shuler and Bear, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A study using a visual orientation discrimination task in mice found pre-stimulus ramping activity specifically in the subpopulation of excitatory cells that encoded the rewarded stimulus, suggestive of reward anticipation.
source: A more recent study using a visual orientation discrimination task in mice found pre-stimulus ramping activity specifically in the subpopulation of excitatory cells that encoded the rewarded stimulus, suggestive of reward anticipation (Poort et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VIP ramping during the inter-stimulus interval may be important for enhancing the responses of excitatory cells to an anticipated change stimulus and consequent reward.
source: VIP ramping during the inter-stimulus interval may be important for enhancing the responses of excitatory cells to an anticipated change stimulus and consequent reward.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: One study demonstrated anticipatory recall of an omitted stimulus in a learned spatiotemporal sequence.
source: One study demonstrated anticipatory recall of an omitted stimulus in a learned spatiotemporal sequence (Gavornik and Bear, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In a virtual navigation paradigm in which mice locomote along a linear track, V1 neurons have been found to predict upcoming stimuli at specific locations, and to signal a deviation from expectation when stimuli are omitted.
source: In a virtual navigation paradigm in which mice locomote along a linear track, V1 neurons have been found to predict upcoming stimuli at specific locations, and to signal a deviation from expectation when stimuli are omitted (Fiser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The ramping signals observed in this study may represent something other than a pure prediction of stimulus timing.
source: This suggests that the ramping signals we observe may represent something other than a pure prediction of stimulus timing.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison with prior studies.

claim: VIP cells may serve to gate the predictive or anticipatory signals documented in excitatory cells.
source: Nonetheless, VIP cells may serve to gate the predictive or anticipatory signals documented in excitatory cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: VIP cells in visual cortex have been shown to be modulated by locomotion and arousal in a context-dependent manner.
source: VIP cells in visual cortex have been shown to be modulated by locomotion and arousal in a context-dependent manner (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2014; Pakan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ramping activity in VIP cells is not simply a reflection of locomotion or arousal.
source: The ramping activity in VIP cells that we observe, however, is not simply a reflection of locomotion or arousal (as indexed by pupil diameter), since the differences in the dynamics of VIP cells cannot be explained by differences in the pattern of animal running behavior or changes in pupil diameter relative to stimulus and omission onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses.

claim: Theoretical work suggests that VIP cells could mediate associative learning and experience-dependent signal routing via disinhibition of local excitatory populations.
source: Theoretical work suggests that VIP cells could mediate associative learning and experience-dependent signal routing via disinhibition of local excitatory populations (Wang and Yang, 2018; Wilmes and Clopath, 2018; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: VIP cells in auditory cortex respond to salient reinforcement signals including reward and punishment.
source: For example, VIP cells in auditory cortex respond to salient reinforcement signals including reward and punishment, and activation of VIP cells enhances the gain of auditory responses (Letzkus et al., 2011; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Inactivation of VIP cells in visual cortex impairs plasticity following monocular deprivation, while activating VIP cells enhances plasticity.
source: Inactivation of VIP cells in visual cortex impairs plasticity following monocular deprivation, while activating VIP cells enhances plasticity (Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the amygdala, VIP cells are necessary for associative memory formation through disinhibition of local pyramidal cells during fear learning.
source: In the amygdala, VIP cells are necessary for associative memory formation through disinhibition of local pyramidal cells during fear learning (Krabbe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VIP cells switching from a stimulus responsive to stimulus suppressed mode depending on past experience may be consistent with a role for VIP cells in enhancing the representation of salient events to facilitate learning and adaptive behavior.
source: Our finding that VIP cells switch from a stimulus responsive to stimulus suppressed mode depending on past experience with an image set may be consistent with a role for VIP cells in enhancing the representation of salient events to facilitate learning and adaptive behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: During sessions with novel images, VIP activity is strongly driven by stimulus presentation, potentially serving to increase the gain of stimulus evoked excitatory responses to salient, novel stimuli.
source: During sessions with novel images, VIP activity is strongly driven by stimulus presentation, potentially serving to increase the gain of stimulus evoked excitatory responses to salient, novel stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: When stimuli are familiar, VIP cells switch from signaling the presence of a stimulus to signaling the absence of a stimulus.
source: When stimuli are familiar, other aspects of the task may become more relevant, such as the unexpected omission of stimuli from a predictable temporal sequence, and VIP cells switch from signaling the presence of a stimulus to signaling the absence of a stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: VIP cells in the visual cortex of passively viewing mice are suppressed by high contrast stimuli and show direction selective responses at low contrast.
source: VIP cells in the visual cortex of passively viewing mice are suppressed by high contrast stimuli and show direction selective responses at low contrast, leading to the proposal that VIP cells are involved in enhancing the gain of weak but salient stimuli (de Vries et al., 2020; Millman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The inter-stimulus and omission ramping activity observed is consistent with the phenomenon of contrast suppression.
source: The inter-stimulus and omission ramping activity we observed, with a decay in the VIP response following onset of familiar images, is consistent with the phenomenon of contrast suppression.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting findings to prior observations.

claim: VIP cells show robust stimulus-evoked responses to novel stimuli, demonstrating that VIP responses are flexible and depend on experience.
source: However our finding that VIP cells show robust stimulus-evoked responses to novel stimuli demonstrates that VIP responses are flexible and depend on experience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: VIP cells represent salient stimuli in a context-dependent manner.
source: These seemingly divergent findings can be unified under the view that VIP cells represent salient stimuli in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation unifying different findings.
